Q: Setting size of CMD windows: Powershell issue after upgrade to Windows 11 A:

I was getting the same error in Windows 10.

I found changing the order of the commands made a difference.

When I run buffersize first I get the error.

powershell.exe -command "&{$w=(get-host).ui.rawui;$w.buffersize=@{width=96;height=100};$w.windowsize=@{width=96;height=18};}"

Exception setting "buffersize": "Cannot set the buffer size because the size specified is too large or too small.
Parameter name: value
Actual value was 96,100."
At line:1 char:26
+ &{$w=(get-host).ui.rawui;$w.buffersize=@{width=96;height=100};$w.wind ...
+                          ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
    + CategoryInfo          : NotSpecified: (:) [], SetValueInvocationException
    + FullyQualifiedErrorId : ExceptionWhenSetting

When run windowsize first no error.

powershell.exe -command "&{$w=(get-host).ui.rawui;$w.windowsize=@{width=96;height=18};$w.buffersize=@{width=96;height=100};}"

In Windows 11, I get the same behavior in Conhost, which is like the Command Prompt in Windows 10, vs. Terminal, which is the new Command Prompt in Windows 11, where the command give no error but doesn't work.

Q: Tkinter RuntimeError: Too early to create image: no default root window A:

I might be 3 years too late, however, the error can be fixed by changing the following line:

img = tk.PhotoImage(imgPath)

to this:

img = tk.PhotoImage(imgPath,master=root)

Q: Moving from C, how can I implement a doubly linked list in C++ using C++ features? A:

The C++ way is to use a standard container. Like std::vector or others.

I once worked on a large mixed codebase that had a lot of copies of your piece of code.

Double linked lists are very common in C because they are very easy to implement.

It was very popular to reinvent the wheel a lot in C due to the limited standard library.

I usually just let the C version live until I needed to modify it. If it worked, that was fine. There are no reason to modify it unless a change was required. If I had to change it I would often replace it with a ` std::vector`, as linked list was usually a convenient but sub optimal choice.

My only real concern when moving away from linked lists was pointer invalidation. It was more than 10 years ago, and checking it manually was a tiresome and error-prone process that nobody wanted to pay for.
